This study investigates whether neutrinos emitted by a future galactic core-collapse supernova could provide evidence for non-standard neutrino interactions (NSI). The analysis considers neutrino flavor evolution within a three-neutrino framework and models how NSI modify propagation through the dense supernova envelope. Particular attention is given to resonant flavor conversions that may occur in the strongly deleptonized inner layers of the star, where the low electron fraction can make matter-induced NSI effects especially significant.

The resulting observational signatures are evaluated for a megaton-scale water Cherenkov detector. Possible indicators of NSI include distinctive modulations in the detected antineutrino energy spectrum as the supernova shock wave crosses relevant resonance regions, spectral changes associated with the evolution of the electron fraction, and additional distortions produced when neutrinos pass through the Earth before reaching the detector. The study also examines whether the prompt neutronization burst of electron neutrinos could remain detectable—or be substantially altered—and thus serve as an independent probe of NSI.

The results show that NSI-induced resonant conversion inside the supernova can generate pronounced, and potentially dramatic, antineutrino spectral features. Such effects may arise for non-universal NSI couplings at the level of a few percent and for flavor-changing NSI strengths larger than a few times \(10^{-5}\). A high-statistics observation of neutrinos from a nearby supernova could therefore offer a sensitive means of testing neutrino interactions beyond the standard framework.

This study investigates the impact of non-standard neutrino interactions (NSI) on three-flavor neutrino propagation through the dense and rapidly evolving environment of a future galactic core-collapse supernova. In addition to the conventional Mikheyev–Smirnov–Wolfenstein matter effect, NSI modify the effective neutrino–matter potential and can generate new resonant flavor conversions deep inside the star. Particular attention is given to these inner-layer resonances and to their interplay with the standard flavor-conversion mechanisms encountered farther out in the stellar envelope.

The analysis considers how the resulting flavor evolution may be reflected in the signal observed by a megaton-scale water Cherenkov detector, whose dominant detection channel is sensitive to electron antineutrinos. Several time- and energy-dependent supernova phenomena are examined, including the passage of the shock wave through resonance regions, changes in the local electron fraction, matter-induced oscillations as neutrinos cross the Earth before reaching the detector, and the short neutronization burst emitted soon after core bounce. Each of these effects can alter the neutrino survival probabilities and may therefore provide a characteristic observational signature of NSI.

The results show that NSI-induced internal resonances can produce pronounced, and in some cases dramatic, distortions in the detected electron-antineutrino energy spectrum. Such effects may occur when the non-universal, flavor-diagonal NSI parameters are at the level of only a few percent, while the relevant flavor-changing interactions need only exceed a few times \(10^{-5}\). Shock-wave propagation and the evolution of the electron fraction can cause these signatures to vary with time, whereas Earth matter effects and the neutronization burst may offer additional means of distinguishing NSI-driven conversion from standard oscillation physics.

Overall, a high-statistics observation of neutrinos from a galactic supernova could provide exceptional sensitivity to non-standard neutrino interactions. The appearance—or absence—of the predicted spectral and temporal features in a megaton water Cherenkov detector would make it possible to probe flavor-changing NSI at extremely small strengths and to test departures from standard three-flavor neutrino propagation in a matter environment inaccessible to terrestrial experiments.
outputs.L5:
## Probing NSI with Megaton-Scale Cherenkov Detectors

Non-standard neutrino interactions (NSI) are hypothetical processes that extend the weak interactions described by the Standard Model. They could modify how neutrinos are produced, detected, or propagated through matter. In particular, NSI may alter neutrino oscillation probabilities by introducing additional interactions between neutrinos and the electrons or quarks found in ordinary matter.

A megaton-scale Cherenkov detector offers a powerful way to investigate these effects. Such a detector contains an enormous volume of transparent material—typically ultrapure water—instrumented with thousands of light sensors. When a charged particle produced by a neutrino interaction travels faster than light can propagate through the medium, it emits a cone of Cherenkov radiation. The pattern, timing, and intensity of this light allow researchers to reconstruct the particle’s direction and energy and, in many cases, identify its type.

The large target mass of a megaton detector provides the high event statistics needed to search for subtle signatures of NSI. By studying atmospheric neutrinos that cross different distances and densities inside Earth, researchers can test whether their oscillations differ from Standard Model predictions. NSI could appear as distortions in the measured energy and zenith-angle distributions, changes in flavor-transition rates, or differences between neutrino and antineutrino behavior.

However, identifying NSI is challenging because their effects can resemble those produced by uncertainties in standard oscillation parameters, Earth’s density profile, or detector performance. Combining megaton Cherenkov data with results from accelerator and reactor experiments can help resolve these degeneracies. Consequently, large Cherenkov observatories are not only instruments for neutrino astronomy and proton-decay searches but also sensitive laboratories for exploring possible new physics in the neutrino sector.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a research paper investigating how non-standard neutrino interactions could be probed using neutrinos from a future galactic supernova.
counterfactuals.output: A future Galactic core-collapse supernova would provide an intense, flavor-rich burst of neutrinos and a unique opportunity to test physics beyond the Standard Model. We investigate the sensitivity of the supernova neutrino signal to non-standard neutrino interactions (NSI) with matter, including flavor-diagonal and flavor-changing couplings. We model neutrino production and flavor evolution through the stellar envelope, incorporating vacuum mixing, standard and non-standard matter effects, and relevant uncertainties in the supernova emission and density profile. The resulting fluxes are propagated to Earth and translated into event spectra for representative next-generation detectors using liquid argon, water Cherenkov, and liquid-scintillator technologies. We examine how NSI modify flavor-conversion resonances, mass-ordering signatures, the neutronization burst, and the time- and energy-dependent event distributions across complementary detection channels. A statistical analysis is used to identify degeneracies among NSI parameters, standard oscillation parameters, and astrophysical uncertainties. We find that combining data from detectors with different flavor sensitivities can substantially improve robustness and distinguish NSI-induced spectral distortions from variations in the source emission. These results demonstrate that a high-statistics Galactic supernova neutrino burst could provide a powerful and complementary probe of non-standard interactions, particularly when timing, spectral, and multi-detector information are analyzed jointly.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a three-neutrino study of NSI effects on supernova neutrino propagation, including inner-envelope resonances, shock waves, electron-fraction evolution, Earth matter effects, and detection in a megaton water Cherenkov detector.
counterfactuals.output:
A three-flavor analysis of supernova neutrino propagation with non-standard neutrino–matter interactions (NSI) finds that even relatively small NSI can qualitatively alter the observable burst.

- **Propagation framework:** NSI add flavor-diagonal and flavor-changing terms, \(\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}\), to the usual matter Hamiltonian. After removing an irrelevant common term, the phenomenology is governed mainly by combinations such as \(\epsilon_{\tau\tau}-\epsilon_{ee}\) and by off-diagonal couplings such as \(\epsilon_{e\tau}\). The resulting evolution is followed through the supernova mantle, any shock-distorted density profile, and—when applicable—the Earth.

- **Inner-envelope or “I” resonance:** At high density, where the electron fraction \(Y_e\) can be small, diagonal NSI may cancel the ordinary charged-current potential and produce a new resonance well inside the conventional H and L MSW layers. Its position is controlled primarily by \(Y_e\), rather than by density alone. A flavor-changing NSI determines how adiabatic the transition is: sufficiently large \(\epsilon_{e\tau}\) can make the I resonance efficient and interchange the electron flavor with a non-electron matter eigenstate. This can reverse the flavor mapping expected from standard oscillations and partly mimic a different mass ordering or a different value of \(\theta_{13}\).

- **Time-dependent electron fraction:** Because \(Y_e(r,t)\) evolves during the explosion, the I-resonance condition may be satisfied only during particular post-bounce epochs. It can therefore switch on or off as the composition changes, producing time-dependent changes in the \(\nu_e\) or \(\bar\nu_e\) spectrum even before shock effects reach the ordinary MSW region. Such features are potentially cleaner NSI indicators than a simple, time-independent spectral swap.

- **Shock-wave effects:** When the outgoing shock crosses the H-resonance region, the density gradient changes rapidly and may create several resonance crossings. The H transition can become temporarily nonadiabatic, generating dips, bumps, or double-dip structures in the detected mean energy and event rate. Multiple crossings may also cause phase-interference oscillations. NSI alter which matter eigenstate reaches the H layer and hence can move these shock signatures between the neutrino and antineutrino channels, suppress them, or make them resemble the signature normally associated with the opposite mass ordering.

- **Earth matter effects:** If the supernova is below the horizon, propagation through the Earth regenerates flavor and superimposes energy-dependent oscillatory modulations on the spectrum. Their presence depends on the mass-eigenstate mixture exiting the star. Because an adiabatic I resonance changes that mixture, NSI can cause Earth effects to appear in a channel where standard oscillations predict none, or remove them where they would normally occur. Comparing shadowed and unshadowed detectors would be especially useful.

- **Megaton water-Cherenkov detection:** The dominant signal is inverse beta decay,
  \[
  \bar\nu_e+p\rightarrow n+e^+,
  \]
  supplemented by elastic scattering and interactions on oxygen. For a Galactic supernova, a megaton-class detector would collect very large statistics, allowing time- and energy-resolved searches for shock-induced dips, evolving I-resonance conversions, and Earth-regeneration wiggles. The \(\bar\nu_e\) channel is particularly powerful, although identifying subtler structures requires adequate energy resolution, time binning, neutron tagging, and control of uncertainties in the primary supernova spectra.

Overall, the study shows that three-neutrino NSI can create a new composition-driven inner resonance and substantially reorganize standard MSW, shock-wave, and Earth-matter signatures. A combination of spectral, temporal, and multi-detector information could distinguish these effects, but degeneracies with the mass ordering, \(\theta_{13}\), supernova emission physics, and the stellar density/composition profile must be treated carefully.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how a galactic supernova could reveal non-standard neutrino interactions through observable features in the electron antineutrino spectrum and the neutronization electron-neutrino burst.
counterfactuals.output:
A Galactic core-collapse supernova would provide an intense, time-dependent neutrino source over tens of seconds. Non-standard neutrino interactions (NSI) with matter could modify flavor conversion inside the star, leaving characteristic signatures in both the \(\bar\nu_e\) energy spectrum and the early \(\nu_e\) neutronization burst.

### How NSI alter flavor evolution

Propagation is governed schematically by

\[
H = H_{\rm vac}+H_{\rm matter}^{\rm SM}
+\sqrt{2}G_F n_f\,\varepsilon_{\alpha\beta},
\]

where \(\varepsilon_{\alpha\beta}\) describe non-standard couplings to electrons or quarks. Diagonal NSI change the relative matter potentials of the flavors, while off-diagonal terms directly induce flavor mixing.

Because a supernova spans enormous ranges of density and electron fraction \(Y_e\), these terms can:

- shift or remove the usual MSW resonances;
- change whether a resonance is adiabatic;
- generate an additional high-density “internal” or \(I\)-resonance when effective flavor potentials cross;
- alter collective flavor conversion and spectral swaps;
- make the flavor outcome differ between neutrinos and antineutrinos.

## Electron-antineutrino spectrum

Most events in water-Cherenkov and liquid-scintillator detectors come from inverse beta decay,

\[
\bar\nu_e+p\rightarrow n+e^+.
\]

The observed flux can be written approximately as

\[
F_{\bar e}(E,t)=\bar p(E,t)F^0_{\bar e}(E,t)
+[1-\bar p(E,t)]F^0_x(E,t),
\]

where \(F^0_x\) is the heavy-flavor flux and \(\bar p\) is the \(\bar\nu_e\) survival probability. NSI modify \(\bar p\), potentially producing:

- an unexpectedly hard or soft \(\bar\nu_e\) spectrum through exchange with the hotter \(\bar\nu_{\mu,\tau}\) flux;
- sharp or broad spectral swaps and split energies;
- dips, shoulders, or step-like features where an NSI-induced resonance changes adiabaticity;
- altered time evolution as the shock wave passes through the relevant density region;
- a flavor pattern normally associated with the opposite neutrino mass ordering.

Such effects could be measured with high statistics in Hyper-Kamiokande, JUNO, and other scintillator or water detectors. Comparing the spectral shape and its time dependence among detectors helps reduce uncertainties in the original supernova emission.

## Neutronization \(\nu_e\) burst

During the first roughly \(10\)–\(30\) ms after core bounce, electron capture produces a short burst that is overwhelmingly \(\nu_e\). Its relative flavor purity makes it a particularly clean probe:

\[
F_e(E,t)\simeq p(E,t)F^0_e(E,t),
\]

because the initial heavy-flavor flux is small during this phase.

In standard three-flavor MSW evolution, the visibility of this burst in the \(\nu_e\) channel depends strongly on the mass ordering and resonance adiabaticity. NSI can instead:

- convert the burst almost completely into \(\nu_{\mu,\tau}\), suppressing the observed \(\nu_e\) peak;
- restore a strong \(\nu_e\) burst where standard oscillations predict suppression;
- produce partial or energy-dependent conversion;
- shift the apparent mass-ordering signature;
- create an unusual burst shape or duration if conversion changes as the density and \(Y_e\) evolve.

A liquid-argon detector such as DUNE is especially sensitive through

\[
\nu_e+{}^{40}{\rm Ar}\rightarrow e^-+{}^{40}{\rm K}^{*}.
\]

### Identifying NSI

The strongest evidence would come from a correlated inconsistency: for example, a neutronization-burst survival pattern incompatible with the known mass ordering, together with \(\bar\nu_e\) spectral swaps or time-dependent features not reproducible by standard MSW and shock-wave conversion. Joint analysis of \(\nu_e\), \(\bar\nu_e\), and flavor-insensitive neutral-current channels would help separate propagation effects from uncertainties in the supernova’s intrinsic neutrino emission.

Thus, the neutronization burst probes NSI through a nearly pure initial \(\nu_e\) signal, while the high-statistics \(\bar\nu_e\) spectrum probes energy- and time-dependent changes in flavor survival.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise technical abstract describing NSI-induced resonant flavor conversion in deleptonized supernova layers and state the approximate interaction strengths required to produce detectable spectral signatures.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract—** Non-standard neutrino interactions (NSI) with matter can generate an internal, nearly energy-independent flavor resonance in the strongly deleptonized layers of a core-collapse supernova. For NSI with down quarks, the resonance occurs when the electron fraction satisfies  
\[
Y_e \simeq \frac{2\epsilon_D}{1+\epsilon_D},
\]
where \(\epsilon_D\) is the relevant difference of diagonal NSI couplings. Thus, profiles reaching \(Y_e\sim10^{-2}\!-\!10^{-1}\) can support resonant \(\nu_e\leftrightarrow\nu_{\mu,\tau}\) conversion for \(\epsilon_D\sim5\times10^{-3}\!-\!5\times10^{-2}\). Flavor-changing couplings control adiabaticity; values \(|\epsilon_{e\mu,e\tau}|\gtrsim10^{-5}\!-\!10^{-4}\), depending on the density gradient, can make the transition efficient. Consequently, diagonal NSI at the \(10^{-2}\) level, accompanied by off-diagonal couplings of at least roughly \(10^{-5}\), may produce observable swaps or distortions in the neutronization burst and cooling-phase spectra. Precise detectability is progenitor-, hierarchy-, and detector-dependent and can be modified by collective oscillations and shock evolution.
